title: Applications of Machine Learning
abstract:
Five sectors — retail, banking & finance, transport, manufacturing, and
consumer internet — and what machine learning actually does inside each one.
For every application this document names the ML task type it reduces to, the
target variable, the features, the metric the business genuinely cares about
(which is rarely accuracy), and the failure mode. The purpose is to build the
translation reflex: hearing a business problem and immediately knowing whether
it is regression, classification, clustering, anomaly detection, or association
rule mining.

blocks.t: The Five Sectors

blocks.cap:
The five sectors named in the notes, with the applications that
 actually run in production inside each.

blocks.t: The skill this topic is really teaching

Nobody will ever hand you a labelled dataset and say "do classification".
They will say "we are losing customers and we do not know which ones".
Your job is the translation. Every application below is annotated with the
task type it reduces to — practise that mapping until it is automatic.

blocks.cap:
Applications mapped onto the task taxonomy from Topic 02. Several
 applications sit in more than one column — that is normal, and choosing the
 framing is the design decision.

blocks.t: Retail — Amazon, Big Bazaar, Flipkart
Recommendation engines

rows: Will this user click / buy this item?
Purchase history, browsing session, item embeddings, time of day, similar users' behaviour
Click-through rate, conversion rate, revenue per session — not accuracy
Filter bubbles; recommending an item the user just bought

blocks.t:
Two families exist. Collaborative filtering recommends what similar
users liked ("people who bought this also bought"). Content-based
filtering recommends items similar to what you liked. Production systems
are hybrids. Roughly 35% of Amazon's revenue is attributed to its recommender.
Demand forecasting

rows: Units of SKU $s$ sold at store $c$ in week $t+1$
Lagged sales, rolling means, holidays, promotions, weather, price, competitor price
WMAPE (Topic 35) — because a 10% error on a high-volume SKU costs far more than 10% on a slow one
Over-forecast $\to$ dead stock; under-forecast $\to$ stockout and lost sale

blocks.t: Why the loss is asymmetric here

The cost of over-stocking (storage, spoilage, markdown) and under-stocking
(lost margin, customer defection) are rarely equal. A symmetric loss like MSE
implicitly assumes they are. Real forecasting systems use quantile loss to
target a specific service level rather than the mean.
Dynamic pricing and market basket analysis

Dynamic pricing is regression onto an optimal price given demand elasticity,
inventory and competitor prices. Market basket analysis is textbook association
rule mining — the "bread and butter" example from Topic 02, run over millions
of transactions with Apriori or FP-Growth, and used to decide physical shelf
placement and bundle offers.
Banking & Finance
Fraud detection

rows: Amount, merchant category, distance from last transaction, time since last transaction, device fingerprint, velocity counts
Recall at a fixed precision — catching fraud matters more than avoiding false alarms, but too many false alarms destroy the customer experience
Fraud is adversarial: the distribution changes because you deployed the model. Permanent concept drift (Topic 03)

blocks.t: Why accuracy is meaningless here

If 0.2% of transactions are fraudulent, a model that predicts "never fraud"
scores 99.8% accuracy and catches nothing. This is the canonical motivation for
precision, recall and F1 (Topic 48) and for the imbalanced-data techniques of
Topic 80.
Credit scoring

Classification (will this applicant default?), but with a hard constraint most ML
problems do not have: it must be explainable. Regulators in most
jurisdictions require an applicant to be told why they were declined.
This is why logistic regression and scorecards survive here despite XGBoost
scoring better — interpretability is a legal requirement, not a preference.
It is also the domain where survivorship bias (Topic 05) bites hardest:
you only observe repayment behaviour for applicants you approved.
Algorithmic trading and AML

Trading is regression or reinforcement learning on price movement, with the
distinctive property that the signal decays as others discover it.
Anti-money-laundering is anomaly detection over transaction graphs, where the
"label" is a suspicious activity report filed months later.
Transport — Ola, Uber
ETA prediction

rows: Route distance, historical speed on each segment, time of day, day of week, weather, live traffic, driver behaviour
MAE in minutes — interpretable to the customer — plus the fraction of trips arriving within the promised window
Systematic under-prediction destroys trust more than over-prediction

blocks.t: Surge pricing, route optimisation, driver matching

Surge pricing is regression onto the price that balances live supply and demand.
Route optimisation is classical operations research (Dijkstra, A*) with ML-predicted
edge weights — a good reminder that ML is often a component of a system
rather than the whole of it. Driver–rider matching is a combinatorial assignment
problem informed by ML-predicted acceptance probabilities and trip durations.
Manufacturing — Tesla
Predictive maintenance

rows: Regression (remaining useful life), classification (will it fail in the next 7 days?), or anomaly detection
Time to failure, or a binary failure flag
Vibration, temperature, current draw, acoustic signature, operating hours, maintenance history
Cost avoided: unplanned downtime vs the cost of unnecessary servicing
Failures are rare, so labels are scarce — exactly the aircraft-engine anomaly-detection setup from Topic 02

blocks.t: Visual defect detection

Classification or object detection on images from the production line. This is
genuinely a deep-learning problem — unstructured data, high volume, features
nobody can articulate. It is the clearest example in this document of a task
where the Topic 01 decision guide sends you to a CNN rather than to XGBoost.
Autonomous driving

The composite application: computer vision (deep learning) for perception,
sensor fusion, and reinforcement learning or imitation learning for the driving
policy — exactly the agent/action/reward/penalty structure from Topic 02.
Consumer Internet — Twitter, Netflix, Meta

head: Application
Task type
Note
rows: Predicts $P(\text{engage})$ per candidate post, then sorts
Extreme class imbalance; errors are politically costly in both directions
Runs at millions of predictions per second; latency budget in single-digit ms
Target definition is the hard part — what counts as "churned"?
Unsupervised; manufactures the label, as in Topic 02

blocks.t: Netflix's own accounting

Netflix has publicly attributed roughly $1B/year of retained revenue to its
recommendation and personalisation systems. The 2009 Netflix Prize — $1M for a
10% RMSE improvement — is also where ensemble methods (Topics 58–70) entered
mainstream practice: the winning entry was a blend of over 100 models.
Reading a Business Problem

head: What the stakeholder says
Task type
Real metric
rows: "How much will we sell next month?"
"What kinds of customers do we have?"
"What should we show this user next?"
"Which of these images has a defect?"

blocks.t: The metric is almost never accuracy

Every row above has a business metric that is not accuracy. Optimising accuracy
when the business cares about recall at a fixed precision produces a model that
looks excellent in your notebook and is rejected in review. Establish the
business metric in the first conversation — this is step 1 of the MLDLC
(Topic 07).
Code: One Application from Each Sector

import numpy as np, pandas as pd
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

# =====================================================================
# RETAIL -- market basket analysis (association rules, no sklearn needed)
# =====================================================================
baskets = [{"bread","butter"}, {"bread","butter","milk"}, {"milk","eggs"},
           {"bread","butter","jam"}, {"bread","milk"}, {"butter","jam"},
           {"bread","butter"}, {"milk","eggs","bread"}]
N = len(baskets)

def support(items):    return sum(items <= b for b in baskets) / N
def confidence(a, b):  return support(a | b) / support(a)
def lift(a, b):        return confidence(a, b) / support(b)

A, B = {"bread"}, {"butter"}
print(f"support {support(A|B):.2f}  confidence {confidence(A,B):.2f}  "
      f"lift {lift(A,B):.2f}")
# lift > 1 => a genuine association, not just two popular items.


# =====================================================================
# BANKING -- fraud detection on a 0.2% positive rate
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.metrics import (classification_report, precision_recall_curve,
                             average_precision_score, accuracy_score)

n = 40_000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 12))
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(3.0 * X[:, 0] + 2.0 * X[:, 1] - 7)))
y = (rng.random(n) < p).astype(int)
print("fraud rate:", y.mean())                       # ~0.2%

Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3, stratify=y, random_state=0)
clf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, class_weight="balanced",
                             random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)

# THE TRAP: accuracy looks fantastic and means nothing
naive = np.zeros_like(yte)
print("accuracy of predicting NEVER FRAUD:", accuracy_score(yte, naive))  # ~0.998

# What the business actually needs: recall at an acceptable precision
prob = clf.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1]
prec, rec, thr = precision_recall_curve(yte, prob)
ok = prec[:-1] >= 0.30                              # tolerate 70% false alarms
if ok.any():
    i = np.argmax(rec[:-1] * ok)
    print(f"at threshold {thr[i]:.3f}: precision {prec[i]:.2f}, recall {rec[i]:.2f}")
print("average precision (PR-AUC):", average_precision_score(yte, prob))


# =====================================================================
# TRANSPORT -- ETA prediction, and why MAE is the right metric
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingRegressor
from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error, mean_squared_error

m = 6000
dist   = rng.uniform(1, 30, m)
hour   = rng.integers(0, 24, m)
rush   = ((hour >= 8) & (hour <= 11)) | ((hour >= 17) & (hour <= 20))
rain   = rng.random(m) < 0.2
eta    = dist * (2.2 + 1.4 * rush + 0.6 * rain) + rng.normal(0, 2, m)

Xt = np.c_[dist, hour, rush.astype(int), rain.astype(int)]
Xtr, Xte, ytr, yte = train_test_split(Xt, eta, test_size=.25, random_state=0)
gb = GradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(Xtr, ytr)
pred = gb.predict(Xte)
print(f"MAE  {mean_absolute_error(yte, pred):.2f} minutes  <- tell the customer this")
print(f"RMSE {mean_squared_error(yte, pred) ** .5:.2f} minutes  <- punishes big misses")


# =====================================================================
# MANUFACTURING -- predictive maintenance as anomaly detection
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest
healthy = np.c_[rng.normal(70, 4, 2000), rng.normal(0.3, .05, 2000)]  # temp, vibration
failing = np.c_[rng.normal(95, 6,   20), rng.normal(0.9, .12,   20)]
machines = np.vstack([healthy, failing])

iso = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=0).fit(healthy)  # fit on NORMAL only
flag = iso.predict(machines) == -1
print(f"caught {flag[2000:].sum()}/20 failing units, "
      f"{flag[:2000].sum()} false alarms out of 2000 healthy")


# =====================================================================
# CONSUMER INTERNET -- customer segmentation (clustering)
# =====================================================================
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rfm = pd.DataFrame({
    "recency":   rng.integers(1, 365, 800),   # days since last purchase
    "frequency": rng.poisson(6, 800),         # orders in the last year
    "monetary":  rng.lognormal(7, 1, 800),    # total spend
})
Z = StandardScaler().fit_transform(rfm)
rfm["segment"] = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit_predict(Z)

# The segments only have value once a human NAMES them:
print(rfm.groupby("segment").agg(
    recency=("recency", "mean"),
    frequency=("frequency", "mean"),
    monetary=("monetary", "mean"),
    size=("recency", "size")).round(1))
# e.g. low recency + high frequency + high monetary  -> "champions"
#      high recency + low frequency                  -> "about to churn"
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
Retail — recommendation engines, demand forecasting, dynamic
 pricing, market basket analysis.

Banking & finance — fraud detection, credit scoring,
 algorithmic trading, AML. Explainability is often a legal requirement.

Transport — ETA prediction, surge pricing, route optimisation,
 driver matching.

Manufacturing — predictive maintenance, visual defect
 detection, autonomous driving.

Consumer internet — feed ranking, content moderation, ad
 targeting, churn prediction, segmentation.

Every application reduces to one of five task types: regression,
 classification, clustering, anomaly detection, association rules.

The business metric is almost never accuracy. Establish it
 before you write any code.

ML is frequently a component of a larger system (ETA feeding a
 routing algorithm), not the whole solution.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Design a churn prediction system for a subscription business.

Start with the target definition, not the model — "churn" must be made
precise (cancelled? inactive 30 days? failed to renew?) and you must fix a
prediction horizon. Then: features from usage frequency, support tickets,
payment failures, tenure, engagement trend. Classification, evaluated by recall
in the top decile, because the retention team can only call a limited number of
customers. Beware leakage — "cancellation request submitted" is not a
feature, it is the label.
Q. Why is accuracy the wrong metric for fraud detection?

Because the classes are extremely imbalanced. At a 0.2% fraud rate, predicting
"never fraud" scores 99.8%. Use precision, recall, F1, and PR-AUC; choose the
operating threshold from the cost of a missed fraud versus the cost of a false
alarm.
Q. A recommender's offline metrics improve but revenue does not. Why?

Several standard causes: offline metrics are computed on logged data biased by
the previous recommender (feedback loop); the model recommends items the
user would have bought anyway, so incremental lift is zero; or the metric
optimised (click) is not the metric that matters (purchase, retention). Only an
A/B test measures the causal effect.
Q. Which application here would you not solve with ML?

Route optimisation. Shortest-path is exactly solvable with Dijkstra or A*; ML's
role is only to predict the edge weights (segment travel times). Using ML for
the search itself would be slower and worse.
Q. Why does credit scoring still use logistic regression?

Regulatory explainability. Declined applicants must be given specific reasons,
and a linear model's coefficients supply them directly. The accuracy that
XGBoost adds does not offset the compliance cost.
